source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2025) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (PNAS Nexus 4(5) pgaf135, published version)
finding: Published version of the reply to Lewis and Mitchell. On shuffled-alphabet letter-string analogies, GPT-4 with self-chosen code execution matched humans; plain GPT-4 did not. Zero-shot chain of thought helped a little but stayed below humans.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Humans vs GPT-4+code: P=0.92 (arXiv v2 reported P=0.496). Humans vs plain GPT-4: P<2e-16. GPT-4 vs GPT-4+CoT: P=0.004; humans vs GPT-4+CoT: P=3e-8; GPT-4+code vs GPT-4+CoT: P=4.4e-5. Code model told not to run code: 22.5% vs GPT-4 alone 21.7% (P=0.73). GPT-4 identified the interval between two letters of the synthetic alphabet in only 10.8% of cases. 38% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% in human data.
quote: the inability of language models to solve these particular reasoning problems is most likely the result of a specific difficulty with counting
limits: Same authors as the original Webb 2023 claim; one model family; GPT-4 only; code use is not human-like; no 2025-26 reasoning model tested; digit matrices not re-run.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent a code sandbox for index and count steps in O7 mapping checks (G2/G3). Chain of thought is not a substitute for exact counting.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) arXiv 2404.13070 v2 reply, extra analyses
finding: Earlier arXiv version of the reply, with extra controls that the code-augmented result is not a training-cutoff or alphabet artifact.
numbers: GPT-4 300 problems per interval size; GPT-4+code 60 per interval size (hand-scored). Interval effect for GPT-4+code P=0.066 (n.s.); humans vs GPT-4 P=8.9e-13 (now re-matched); humans vs GPT-4+code P=0.496. New alphabet vs original, GPT-4+code P=0.52. Old vs new GPT-4 engine P=0.12. 23/50 (46%) GPT-4+code errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% in human data. Extend-sequence, interval 2: 9/10 wrong because code was not used to find the interval.
limits: Only 60 hand-scored code problems per condition. The human-vs-code P value changed between arXiv v2 (0.496) and the published version (0.92); quote the published figure.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure case: if the model does not choose to run code, it still fails. The scaffold should force a code step for any index or count operation.

source: Liu, Li, Fang, Xu, He, Tan (2025) Rethinking the Role of Prompting Strategies in LLM Test-Time Scaling (arXiv 2505.10981)
finding: First equal-budget comparison that includes analogical prompting (AnP, Yasunaga style). Under majority voting with matched sample count or token cost, plain chain of thought wins as budget grows. AnP is the weakest of the strategies on most models.
numbers: 6 LLMs x 8 strategies x 6 benchmarks (GSM8K, GSM-Hard, MATH-500, 3 MMLU subsets). Limit accuracy, CoT vs AnP: Qwen2.5-7B 88.2 vs 81.3; LLaMA-3-8B 71.3 vs 68.2; GLM-4-9B 83.1 vs 77.0; Phi-3.5-mini 81.4 vs 77.6; Gemini-1.5-Flash 91.3 vs about 90.9 (table text garbled); GPT-4o-mini DiP 89.9, CoT 90.0. AnP has more hard questions than CoT (Qwen 18.4% vs 11.6%).
quote: complicated prompting strategies with superior initial performance gradually fall behind simple Chain-of-Thought
limits: Maths and MMLU science only, small and mid models, no reasoning models. AnP here is the generic prompt, not a two-source O7 pipeline with a written common rule. Compute matched by samples or token price.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 1: at equal compute a single-pass analogy prompt does not beat plain sampling on maths. O7 must be tested against best-of-N on structure-bound tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies (arXiv 2406.06461)
finding: At a matched budget of 20 queries or 10k tokens per question, CoT self-consistency matches or beats multi-agent debate and Reflexion on almost all tasks. Analogical prompting was not tested. Tree of Thoughts wins only on Game of 24 with GPT-4 and at high cost.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral, Llama-2-70B, Mixtral; GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, CSQA, HotpotQA, Game of 24. ToT on Game of 24 (100 items): GPT-4 proposer + GPT-3.5 evaluator $33.53, 72%; GPT-4 evaluator $159.87, 76%; beam 1 $49.90, 65%.
limits: Per-point accuracies only in figures. Does not cover analogy.
agent_relevance: Sets the baseline the scaffold must beat: a plain self-consistency arm at the same token count. Log tokens per arm.

source: Google DeepMind authors (2025) Enhancing Reasoning with Collaboration and Memory (arXiv 2503.05944)
finding: Analogical prompting beats zero-shot CoT on 2 of 3 tasks with Gemini Pro and Ultra and is not hurt by random memory. Agents given different example sets beat self-consistency with the same total exemplars in most pairs.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Pro/Ultra; FOLIO, RACO, TSO; 6 runs. ZCoT vs AP self-consistency: FOLIO Pro 47 vs 56, Ultra 49 vs 53; RACO Pro 84 vs 90, Ultra 80 vs 83; TSO Pro 49 vs 46, Ultra 78 vs 49 (CoT better on TSO). Matched table (5 agents, 15 exemplars) varied-context vs SC: FOLIO Pro 56 vs 51; RACO Pro 91 vs 82; TSO Ultra 88 vs 64; RACO Ultra SC 62 vs varied 51. Random retrieval generally beat similarity retrieval.
limits: AP greedy (1 call) vs ZCoT (2 calls) not call-matched; only the varied-vs-SC rows are matched. No tokens reported. Old models, three small tasks.
agent_relevance: Weak support that a different analog or example set per sample beats repeating one context at equal sample count. Test in the scaffold.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench: Benchmarking the Identification of Abstract and Long-context Analogies (EMNLP 2024, arXiv 2402.12370)
finding: Picking the analogous story from 4 options works for 1-sentence stories but falls as stories lengthen. Retrieving analogs from a bank of 200 stories is near random for GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 2.
numbers: T1 accuracy 1/10/30 sentences: GPT-4 89.1/66.5/60.7; GPT-3.5 65.3/46.4/30.8; Claude v2 68.2/30.2/25.9; Tulu2-70B 71.8/51.2/31.5; LLaMA2-70B 55.6/39.2/29.5; humans 96.0/72.5/73.3; random 25. T2: top-10 of 200 stories (bank about 4K tokens at 1 sentence, 110K at 30 sentences); both models near random except GPT-4 Turbo at 1 sentence. No human baseline for T2. No CoT tried.
limits: Text gap figure (28.8%) disagrees with the table (12.6); T2 numbers not readable in the text; 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Warning for memory-store retrieval of analogs: unaided long-context recall of the right case is near chance. Retrieval needs an index, not model reading of a long bank.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: Deriving Story-level Analogies from LLMs (arXiv 2310.12874)
finding: LLMs pick hard negatives (high noun overlap, wrong structure) more often than the true analogy. Embedding and LLM scorers correlate almost zero with human analogy scores.
numbers: 4-option multiple choice, human 85.7%, chance 25%. 0-shot: ChatGPT 35.8, GPT-3.5 44.2, LLaMA-65B 27.7, FlanT5-xxl 45.0. Share of choices on hard negatives: LLaMA-65B 59.7, ChatGPT 59.5, GPT-3.5 55.8, FlanT5 37.2; on the correct analogy 28.6/32.4/37.1/45.4; easy negatives under 20%. Analogy-score Spearman: humans about 62.5; best RoBERTa-CL 25.0; OpenAI-ada 0.7, GPT-3.5 0.9, ChatGPT 2.3.
limits: 2023 models; story-level data built by LLM then annotated.
agent_relevance: Supports O6 stripping of surface content before matching: noun overlap is the main lure. Add hard-negative items (same nouns, wrong structure) to the harness.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as Models for Analogical Reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145:104676; arXiv 2406.13803 v3)
finding: Word-to-symbol mapping tasks that need re-representation of meaning. Claude 3 Opus tracks humans closely in most conditions; GPT-4 and Llama-405B fall behind in some. All three are pulled by semantic distractors more than humans.
numbers: 194 human students (132 Semantic Structure, 62 Semantic Content), 6-18 per condition, 4 questions per quiz. Versus Only-RHS, irrelevant left-hand semantics cost humans a modest drop; Claude 3 about -0.5, GPT-4 about -0.8, Llama-405B about -0.4 (match-to-reference). Random-final conditions: Claude 3 about -0.5, GPT-4 -0.6 and -0.4. Numeric condition: humans and Claude 3 about 0.7, GPT-4 and Llama-405B about 0.35 (GPT-4 z=-3.065, p=0.002). Humans fell 0.7 to 0.4 in dual-attribute (p=0.002), models did not. Chain of thought on Claude 3 gave weak gains.
limits: Small cells, mostly undergraduates, 2024 models, match-to-reference not accuracy. Not a test of re-description before mapping.
agent_relevance: Distractor pull persists in the best 2024 models, so O6 should drop surface cues. A direct test of structural re-description is still missing (gap 9 stays open).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas (arXiv 2506.20803)
finding: Independent downstream check on LLM novelty claims. 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing a randomly assigned idea. LLM ideas scored higher at ideation but lost the advantage after execution.
numbers: N=19 human ideas, N=24 AI ideas. Ideation means (human/AI): novelty 4.912/5.778, excitement 4.404/5.653, effectiveness 4.833/6.003, overall 4.596/5.382. Execution means: novelty 4.903/4.729, excitement 4.482/3.896, effectiveness 4.782/4.125, overall 3.968/3.406 (all n.s., FDR p 0.175-0.586). Gap (execution minus ideation) for AI ideas -1.049, -1.760, -1.879, -1.976; human ideas -0.010, +0.078, -0.052, -0.628. Difference p=0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004 (FDR).
limits: Small N (43 projects), NLP prompting topics, executors varied in skill and effort.
agent_relevance: Judge-rated novelty is a weak signal. Rank analogical ideas by cheap execution (code run), not by LLM novelty ratings (G8).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) ideation vs execution score correlation (appendix D of 2506.20803)
finding: Review scores before execution barely predict scores after execution. For AI ideas the excitement score is moderately negatively correlated.
numbers: AI ideas Pearson r: novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092. Human ideas: -0.084, 0.205, 0.022, 0.158. N=24 AI, 19 human.
agent_relevance: Idea-stage judgement, including the agent's own, is not evidence of eventual quality; keep an execution gate.

source: Barakat and Kochmar (2026) Teaching Through Analogies: A Modular Pipeline for Educational Analogy Generation (arXiv 2605.24211)
finding: Source finding from relational descriptions: adding sub-concepts (the relational parts of a system) to the query lifts embedding retrieval; LLM re-ranking on gold sub-concepts gives the best top-1 pick. Absolute hit rates stay low.
numbers: 7 embedding models, 12 LLMs. SCAR average retrieval 0.557 to 0.673 with sub-concepts (OpenAI-Large 0.710 to 0.792; OpenAI-Small 0.677 to 0.780). Selection Hit@1: gold sub-concepts re-rank 24.5%, background 22.2%, gold+background 20.8%, embedding-only 19.5%, generated sub-concepts 18.2%, names only 17.5%. Hit@2/3 embedding-only best (30.5%, 40.0%). Generation Hit@20 best: Gemini-2.5 75.4%, GPT-OSS-120B 75.3%. 7 graduate-student annotators, 165 judgements. Background text added at most +0.006.
limits: Educational analogies (concept to familiar system), not problem solving. Gold sub-concepts are human annotations; model-generated ones only slightly beat names. Claude Sonnet 4.6 used as judge.
agent_relevance: Relational descriptions help, but model-written ones add little (18.2 vs 17.5 Hit@1). Gap 4 partly closed: relation-aware retrieval beats names but top-1 stays about one in four to five.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) arXiv 2402.08955 page check for later evaluations
finding: Only v1 (Feb 2024) is listed and its abstract covers three GPT models. No reasoning-model, o1 or later evaluation is attached.
numbers: Humans stay high; GPT models decline sharply on the counterfactual set (details in c04).
limits: A web search for o1 or DeepSeek-R1 on counterfactual letter strings, run this session, returned only the Lewis, Mitchell and Webb papers, so no 2025-26 reasoning-model result was found. Arxiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar search APIs were rate-limited, so absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for reasoning models; plan an in-house run on altered alphabets with and without a code tool.

source: Das and Balke (2025) From Prototypical to Relational: How LLMs Navigate Complex Analogies (INLG 2025)
finding: Search-result summary only: 1,210 four-way multiple-choice items where every distractor shares at least one relation with the stem; authors report limits in structured relational reasoning.
limits: Not opened; no accuracy figures read.
agent_relevance: Possible source of hard-negative items for a harness; open before use.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach, Schunn (2013) Learning Through Case Comparisons: A Meta-Analytic Review (Educational Psychologist 48(2):87-113)
finding: Existing meta-analysis of case-comparison learning, the large-scale test of Gick and Holyoak style comparison. Only bibliographic metadata was read (Crossref: 84 references; Semantic Scholar: 333 citations). Abstract and effect sizes were not readable: publisher page returned 403 and the Pitt PDF link returned a non-PDF.
limits: Gap 8 stays open: effect size not verified. Do not cite a number for it.
agent_relevance: Open the Pitt copy in a later session; it is the right source for the two-case comparison effect size.

source: Webb et al. PNAS Nexus 2025, discussion of re-representation
finding: Authors argue the code-augmented model re-represented permuted-alphabet problems as numerical index problems on its own, which they compare to re-representation in insight problems. They say the result applies only to analogical reasoning and that the link to human mechanisms is open.
numbers: Model generated its own code; no task-specific instructions on position or interval size.
limits: Authors' interpretation; first author at Microsoft Research and funded by Azure (declared).
agent_relevance: Supports O6 as re-description into a code-checkable form, but it is framing, not a controlled test.

source: Liu et al. (2025) adaptive scaling and strategy selection (same paper as d03)
finding: Spending samples only on hard questions and picking the best strategy per question helps most, but only with oracle labels; models cannot yet do it alone.
numbers: LLaMA-3-8B: GSM8K Majority@10 86.0 to 97.4 and MATH-500 15.2 to 61.0 with oracle adaptive scaling plus strategy choice; GPQA and AIME from just over 30% to 75.7% (oracle).
limits: Oracle difficulty labels; upper bound, not deployable.
agent_relevance: When to invoke O7 per question is where a gain could sit, but the selector is unsolved. Test a cheap trigger such as disagreement among samples.
